That's an option, but it might be easier and ultimately faster to just play as Zeus, particularly because reloading the map every time you get shot might get tiring. Zeus is essentially a GM mode for ARMA, and it is intended to allow a player to, in realtime, build a mission as other players are playing it, but it works just as well to screw around as one player. You can put people/vehicles/buildings/whatever down on the map, give them orders, edit their equipment, take direct control of them, whatever. And crucially, if a guy you're mind-controlling gets killed, you just go back to being Zeus and you can take over the next guy in line without restarting anything. Zeus is helped out a lot by the "Ares" mod, available on the steam library, which introduces a bunch of shortcuts for commonly done but normally tedious tasks. There are built in Zeus "missions" (empty maps with Zeus enabled) you can play, but they all have a sort of regenerating cap on how often you can do stuff to keep the Zeus player from going too crazy, if that starts bothering you you might want to grab a version (or make your own if you're up for it) that doesn't have that cap included.

So you could, for example, as Zeus spawn a couple of opposing rifle squads on opposite sides of a valley, set the time to dusk so the autorifle tracers stand out, spawn an AH-9 and take control of it and fly around raining rockets on those who displease you. As their numbers thin, or if you get shot down, just keep on adding guys and taking control of whatever seems interesting.

I also recommend DUWS as a good starting point to get familiar with the game and screw around. There are a bunch of them available on various maps and with support for various extra content, but this one is pretty good because it supports the developer-made virtual arsenal, which is hugely better than the player-made VAS. All the DUWS versions have the same core: You pick a base location, you buy some equipment and such with points, then you do randomly generated missions to get more points. There are servers online that are running maps that work in a similar way ("Invade and Annex" mission type), but they tend to devolve into a helicopter load of people with ridiculously powerful gear combinations (.338 MGs with computer-controlled thermal sights and lock-on launchers on their backs) running around completing every mission in about a minute. Some servers have limits on that sort of gear to make it more interesting.

In terms of popular content, RHS has a couple of mods that basically add modern day Russian and American forces into the game (and they have some pretty great trailers), if the near-future stuff in default ARMA doesn't tick your box.

And while I'm mentioning popular ARMA youtube clips, there's the whole Dslyecxi channel, but this may be a good starting place.

People are also hugely into "Altis Life", where I guess you roleplay or something, and some people are cops and they try to arrest other people for breaking the law? I'm not hugely up on it because it's not my thing, but consistently those servers seem the most populated, so I guess people like it. The "King of the Hill" servers are also very popular- a bunch of players get dropped into the map, they have to scavenge gear, the area they're allowed to be in shrinks, and eventually one guy makes it out alive, and the map restarts. Exile is about doing some survival style stuff, some servers have zombies and some just have multiple teams, events get spawned to spark conflict. But if you want something where you get killed a bit less by people who have been playing the game 500 hours more than you, I recommend looking for a zeus mission with some players. Those are basically always cooperative, though the quality of the guy playing Zeus can have a huge impact on how fun it is to play.

After that, you should look up the traditional Chinese music notation. After looking at it for a few minutes, it all started to make sense to me. That notation doesn't bother with the key signature at all (from the few examples I've seen), it just has the set of notes and numbers them 1 through 8, and it tells you which number to play with an indicator for how long. In many ways it's the same as modern notation, but it skips a lot of the things that shouldn't quite be there.

I play violin and a bit of piano, and I hate standard notation, especially for piano. Note placements on the staff are different for each hand, middle c is off the staff for both hands, and it doesn't even have the right number of spaces for the number of notes in an octave. That last bit makes it harder to transpose the sheet music up or down an octave.
